III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00459

The key to that interpretation lies here in Suhrawardi’s own person: it is in him that Islamic spirituality demonstrates its capacity to embrace the exemplary visions of Hermes, Zoroaster, and Plotinus. Suhrawardi has confided to us the personal secret of that capacity: the access, granted him by divine grace, to the “Eastern Source.” That Source is precisely what he means by the term Khorrâh, the Persian equivalent of the Avestan Xvarnah: the Light of Glory, the blazing radiance of heavenly Light, the source of “Eastern knowledge.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00460

Access to this source enabled him to build his Eastern Theosophy. As he has emphatically warned us, this theosophy does not arise from theoretical knowledge. It is drawn from an experience of Light: the calling of the “Easterners,” the Ishraqiyun, and of everyone to whom that name can rightly apply. The idea of Ishraq, or Illumination, whose essential features we have already explored, ultimately coincides with the idea of Xvarnah. Suhrawardi insists that the sources (yanabi’) of Ishraq are the very sources of Xvarnah.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00461

The Orient of Light, Eastern Light, and the Light of Glory are different names for one and the same source of all sources. And that is indeed what is at stake: the source of sources. Suhrawardi repeats throughout his writings that the experience of these Lights is not theoretical knowledge about an object, not the formation of a concept, and not an image constructed from a concept. It is what makes all the knowledge of Eastern theosophy possible and gives that knowledge its foundation. Light is not itself the object of vision; Light is what makes vision possible.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00462
This is not the place to attempt a linguistic history of the word Xvarnah, a task in any case beyond our competence.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00463

But a few indications are needed to situate the principal texts in which Suhrawardi uses its Persian form. As noted above, khorrah is the Persian form derived from the Avestan Xvarnah, corresponding to the northern Middle Persian, or Pahlavi, form Xvarrah. The same term also appears in Persian as farr, derived not from Avestan but from the Old Persian of the Achaemenids (farnah), through the southern Pahlavi form farrah. This element appears in the names of certain Iranian rulers, preserved in Greek transcriptions such as Artaphernes, Pharnadates, and Gondophares.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00464

Since Anquetil-Duperron, Iranologists have proposed at least twenty descriptions, definitions, or translations of the word. In practice, much the same terms recur: glory, radiance, splendour, sovereignty, blazing majesty, supernatural and victorious fire, halo, and so on.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00465

In short, they evoke light, glory, and sovereignty: a radiance beyond the senses that nevertheless shows itself through certain signs in the world of the senses. There have, of course, been attempts to demonstrate that “originally” the word had a purely practical meaning, without mystical significance. I strongly suspect that explanations of this kind always conceal some unacknowledged—or unconscious—philosophical assumption. At any rate, they are of no use to us here. Supposing lead has been transformed into gold, it is the gold that interests us. In Suhrawardi, his commentators, and his disciples, the word khorrah has a perfectly clear and precise meaning, entirely faithful to the tradition.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00466

The best way to sum it up is to preserve both its tangible and its mystical meaning. We may say with J. Darmesteter that Xvarnah is “the halo of light and divine inspiration that descends upon the saints; it is the heavenly principle that gives the person invested with it power, virtue, genius, and happiness. It is divine good fortune.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00467

We must also emphasize, as Émile Benveniste does, the connection between Xvarnah and the very principle of being and life. Xvarnah is “a luminous sign of heavenly favour and of power delegated by the gods”; it symbolizes “radiant prosperity,” but is also “an inner agent of vitality, the force that binds a being to existence.” This connection is essential if we are to understand the meanings gathered over time under the name Xvarnah, and how the idea entered Islamic gnosis—not only in Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy but earlier still in Ismaili gnosis.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00468

It brings together the Light of Glory (Greek doxa) and personal Destiny (Greek tykhê). Their fusion was chiefly the work of Zurvanism, the religious tradition centred on eternal Time. We have already seen this tradition reappear, in dramatically altered form, in Ismaili accounts of the origin of the cosmos. We may even say that the fusion is symbolized in the Aramaic ideogram used to represent Xvarnah in the Pahlavi texts of Zoroastrianism.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00469
We must now briefly review several facts bearing on this point.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00470

In different Greek texts, Xvarnah is rendered by two words: doxa, meaning glory, and tykhê, meaning destiny or fortune. For anyone studying how religious realities are experienced and manifested, the pairing is already full of meaning. It helps explain the forms in which Xvarnah appears, the distinct personal figures it can take, and the qualities attributed to it. It also helps us understand how Xvarnah can be encountered as a person belonging to the world of Light. We should not be too quick to call this “mythology.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00471

What is at issue is a reality beyond the senses, yet entirely concrete and individual. We need to bring out these features now so that we can recognize them when they reappear in Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00472

Zoroastrian books written in Pahlavi employ a curious system known as uzvaresh. Probably surviving from a time when documents of the Persian imperial chancery were written in Aramaic, this system writes certain words in Aramaic rather than Pahlavi. Readers see the Aramaic word but pronounce its Pahlavi equivalent. Aramaic words enclosed in this fashion thus function as ideograms—there are about six hundred of them—and scholars of Pahlavi know how much labour they have caused. Now the Pahlavi word xvarnah is written with the Aramaic word gaddeh, meaning destiny or fortune.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00473

The connection we have just described is therefore already present in the written sign itself. This Glory-Destiny (xvarnah-tykhê) appears on certain coins from Bactria, personified sometimes as a male figure and sometimes as a female one. Compare the Syrian god Gad, the Roman Dea Fortuna, and the Greek Agathê Tykhê. The aspect of radiant Glory is also represented on these coins, sometimes by a halo and sometimes by flames rising from the shoulders.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00474

This personification is itself rooted in a characteristic capacity of Zoroastrian thought: the ability to perceive beings and things by encountering them in the person of their “angel,” their heavenly archetype. In other words, to perceive what they are in their essence by perceiving who they are. This is how Xvarnah itself is apprehended as one of the personal figures inhabiting the subtle world of Light, one of the Yazatas, the beings “Worthy of Worship.” Like every being of that subtle heavenly world, Xvarnah possesses a Fravarti (Persian foruhar): its archetype or “angel,” known as “Infinite Light.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00475

And like the other figures of Zoroastrian angelology, Xvarnah can remain a spiritual being in its own right—a distinct reality in the spiritual world (menok)—while being wholly present in each of the individual forms through which it comes into relation with the materially manifested world (getik). The heavenly Figure is both itself and the energy it unfolds and invests in a being of the material world.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00476

Already in the Avesta, we find three forms in which Xvarnah takes shape in the earthly world: (1) the Light of Glory of the Aryans (Airyanem Xvareno), belonging to the knights of the Iranian epic and to the heroes and heroines of the Zoroastrian faith; (2) the royal Light of Glory (Kavaem Xvareno), belonging to Vishtaspa, Zoroaster’s protector, and to the kings of the Kayanid dynasty; and (3) the Light of Glory of Zoroaster himself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00477
We shall find all three categories faithfully represented in Suhrawardi, enriched with shades of meaning that had gathered around the term during the centuries before it reached him.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00478

The accounts of Zoroaster’s Xvarnah are especially illuminating for the study of religious experience. In one version, Xvarnah descends as a Flame from Infinite Light and enters Zoroaster’s mother at the moment of her own birth. In another, Zoroaster’s Fravarti—his “heavenly being”—and his Xvarnah unite to form the child Zoroaster. Or else the Amharaspands, the “archangels,” place them in earthly substances—hom and milk—that will nourish his parents. Later, Zoroaster’s Xvarnah is preserved in the waters of Lake Kansaoya, from which rises the mountain of dawns, Mons Victorialis, the Mountain of Victory.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00479

A multitude of Fravartis keep watch over it. At the end of our cycle, our Aeon, a young woman will enter the waters of the mystical Lake. The Light of Glory will become present within her body, and she will conceive “the one who is to subdue all the evil spells of demons and human beings.” None of this, of course, belongs to the anatomy or physiology of the physical body. As an element of Zoroastrian understanding of the human being, Xvarnah belongs to the “body of light,” or, to use a simplifying expression, the “subtle body.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00480

The nature of Xvarnah as the blaze of primordial Light; its transmission through the archangels; its anticipated reappearance in the future Saoshyant, who will bring our Aeon to a close—all of this calls for comparison with the motif of the “Muhammadan Light” (Nur Muhammadi) contemplated in Shiite teachings about prophecy (see above, Book I). That Light is transmitted mystically from the heavenly fullness of divine beings, the Pleroma, to Adam; then from prophet to prophet until Muhammad; and finally to the last Imam of the Muhammadan era.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00481

There is more: the supernatural process leading to the birth of the child Zoroaster corresponds closely to the process that precedes the birth of the holy Imams. Here we can do no more than point out these striking parallels.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00482

Some years ago, however, we were able to identify equally clear traces of the Xvarnah motif in a fourth/tenth-century Ismaili theosopher, Abu Ya'qub Sejestani. He invited us to treat the Arabic word jadd by reading it as the Persian bakht—destiny, allotted fortune—just as the Aramaic ideograms in Pahlavi require a reader to do. In Pahlavi commentaries on the Avesta, xvarrah is likewise interpreted as bakht. The way forward was then clear, for Abu Ya'qub’s descriptions allow us to recognize in the three archangels of Ismaili gnosis—Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel—three distinct manifestations of Xvarnah: the Aura Gloriae, or Doxa-Sophia, Glory-Wisdom.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00483
We cannot repeat the details here.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00484

Let us simply note that, because Abu Ya'qub is speaking of the spiritual gift bestowed upon prophets and Imams, his account corresponds particularly closely to what Suhrawardi says (as we shall see below) about royal Xvarnah: the Light of Glory that invests the “representative of God on His earth.” Since this is the source of the sacred gift that makes the Pole or Imam what he is, it matters little, to Suhrawardi as to Shiite thinkers, whether the Imam is hidden or openly present and recognized. Worldly authority is not what makes him the Pole and the Imam. His spiritual gift endures, whatever human beings may do.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00485

Yet the Light of Glory has manifestations and individual forms other than the full royal and priestly spiritual gift. We recalled above that it is the power that constitutes a being of light and holds that being together. In this sense, the Glory means the soul itself: the soul as pre-existing in one way or another, as the eternal archetype and standard of an earthly individual. It is the pre-existing energy that makes this being an individual and spreads a protective radiance around it. It cannot be detached from that being without placing the being in danger; nor can the being seek to go beyond it or deny it without destroying its own existence.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00486

Thus the Glory takes on the features of an eternal Companion of light, who appears both as the goal and as the guide toward that goal. The “Glory” allotted to a being is therefore truly that being’s “Destiny.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00487

All at once, a whole group of images and ideas associated with Zurvan—as absolute Time, eternal Time—begins to reveal how they fit together. More precisely, we might speak of a play of figures shining through one another, attested by texts from different traditions. Zurvan appears at once as Light of Glory and as Destiny, making him, so to speak, the ideal meeting place of the two meanings whose fusion concerns us here.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00488

Put very briefly, the Greek equivalents of these ideas tend to bring this interplay into focus around a particular Figure: the Agathos Daimon of Hermeticism, the Good Spirit, who in each instance becomes a guardian Angel or heavenly counterpart. This appearance of one figure through another agrees with an identification we can already discern in Zurvan: he is also Wisdom-Daena, at once the divine Wisdom of the Zoroastrian religion—its Sophia—and the heavenly Self of the believer. For Zurvan is essentially many-formed. He is the Aeon, eternal Time, the pantomorphos theos, the God who assumes every form.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00489
It follows that each figure in which the Aeon reveals itself is supremely fitted to say to the initiate: “I am your eternity”—your Aeon.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00490

Here lies the secret of the image that brings together the Light of Glory and Destiny in a single Form, a single Figure. We find the same union when Destiny (tykhê) is identified with the Figure that dominates the religious horizon of Hermeticism: Agathos Daimon. He is at once Nous, the divine Intelligence of Hermeticism, and the personal good daimon of Hermes and of the Hermetic initiate. He is the daimon paredros: the heavenly companion or counterpart, the guardian “Angel” of the person who is his earthly counterpart. It is precisely this Agathos Daimon whom Suhrawardi knows and invokes as the “Perfect Nature” (al-Tiba’ al-tamm). That is the name of the “Form of light” which, in the tradition of Islamic Hermeticism, appears to Hermes and “casts knowledge into him” (see below, Section 5 and Chapter VI).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00491

Let us also note here that a trace of this “Perfect Nature” can be found in a Shiite hadith concerning the First Imam. We may recall, too, the “Form of light” that joins the Ismaili initiate during initiation, which we have shown elsewhere to be a reminiscence of Manichaean teaching.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00492

Set out so quickly, these ideas may seem hopelessly entangled. Certainly, the ways in which these religious worlds overlap and meet in such images form one of the most complex chapters in the study of religions. So long as we are content to speak too easily of “syncretism,” everything may appear arbitrary and confused.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00493

But if we try to discover what a person’s faith intends, and how it gives shape to an entire world, then that faith itself—the thing supposedly “inexplicable”—becomes the explanation. Hermeticism and Zoroastrianism meet in Suhrawardi’s personal faith in a way whose ultimate secret lies in Suhrawardi himself. Their meeting is announced by his use of two distinctive ideas: the Zoroastrian Light of Glory and the Hermetic “Perfect Nature.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00494

Suhrawardi bears witness to the first by recounting a vision, and to the second in one of the most beautiful psalms in his “Book of Hours.” They come together through an underlying idea that emerges fully into view when the Light of Glory is identified with personal Destiny.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00495

To sum up the facts we have reviewed: (1) In Zoroastrianism, Zurvan is the infinite Time of Ohrmazd’s Religion (Daena, Persian Din). That Religion is Ohrmazd’s path, eternally vibrating in the Light. It is divine Wisdom or Sophia, the “robe” and eternal Time of Ohrmazd. It is also the Figure that, after death, presents itself to the Zoroastrian soul that has fought and won its battle, as the soul’s heavenly Self, its Self of light.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00496

Thus the soul embodied on earth recognizes its heavenly partner or counterpart in a Figure through whom the Figure of eternal Time shines. (2) In the Corpus Hermeticum, the Aeon, eternal Time, likewise appears as a distinct divine reality, a Power of God identical with Wisdom-Sophia, the active, creative Soul of the world. This World Soul is the mother of Anthropos: the initiate who has been reborn and has brought forth his “immortal body” (athanaton soma). This assurance of immortality is bound precisely to attaining, or receiving, the daimon paredros: the heavenly “Angel” or companion, a free gift obtained through prayer and initiation.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00497

The parallel is striking. Zurvan and the Aeon each take the form of personal Destiny. In Zoroastrianism, this is the angel Daena-Sophia, who is at once a distinct manifestation of the Zoroastrian religion and the personal “angel” of the Zoroastrian believer. In Hermeticism, it is Agathos Daimon, who is at once a divine manifestation and the daimon paredros, the personal angel of every initiate.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00498
We can thus see how Zoroastrianism and Hermeticism meet in a single fundamental image.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00499

The common element, in Suhrawardi’s thought, is what binds the vision of the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, to the form of light called the “Perfect Nature”—a person’s own destiny, since it is at once the initiate’s “father” and “child.” And this union opens onto a vast horizon.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00500

Later we shall consider the studies that have connected the Zoroastrian idea of the Xvarnah with the Holy Grail of Western tradition, and the figure of Kay Khosraw with that of Parsifal. Other studies, meanwhile, have traced the sources of Wolfram von Eschenbach’s Parsifal to the Corpus Hermeticum. What emerges from these lines of research is the idea of a meeting of traditions—a meeting that, in Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy, has already taken place.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00501

That meeting is already apparent in the imagery of the Xvarnah, whether imagined or actually depicted. Its triumphant visions are precisely what will find expression in the language of the shaykh al-Ishrâq, the master of Illumination. The figures shine through at the threshold between the visible and invisible worlds, surrounded by an aura of victory: the victory of the believer, the initiate, or the mystic undergoing the rebirth inscribed in his or her destiny. The victorious power inherent in the Xvarnah—at once Light of Glory and Destiny—becomes an attribute of the person it invests.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00502

In Mazdean theosophy, this Gloria victrix, or conquering Glory, appears in the person of the angel Ashi Vanuhi, “daughter of Ohrmazd, sister of the archangels, Spirit of wisdom.” A majestic and proud figure, she is, in the language of sacred imagery, a sister to the Nikai, the winged figures of Victory in Greek sculpture. Those figures, chiefly through Gnostic influences, were among the sources of the earliest Christian images of angels. Ashi Vanuhi both possesses and bestows the Xvarnah; yet she is also Victory itself, its triumphant Fire.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00503

Glory and Destiny converge in her person: the Aura Gloriae of a being of light. Mithraism, too, understood her as tykhê, destiny, in the sense of Fortuna victrix, victorious Fortune—Glory and Fortune as one. Her meeting with Zoroaster in Erân-Vêj, a famous episode of the Avesta (Yasht XVII), is an exemplary event taking place “at the centre of the world.” As such, it prefigures—and makes possible—the believer’s meeting after death with her sister Daênâ, who is the believer’s own “victorial power.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00504

We have recalled these images and scenes because they embody the qualities of the Xvarnah that give Suhrawardi’s vocabulary its characteristic tone. Central to them is the idea of victory, of triumphant power (Pahlavi pêrôzih), inherent in beings of light. Persian and Arabic texts offer many equivalents: greatness and beauty (’azamat o zibâî, bahâ’), light (nûr), radiant joy (bahjat), and others. (Here one might recall Repanse-de-joie, the name of the Grail queen in Wolfram’s poem.) When writing in Arabic, Suhrawardi chiefly uses qahr, meaning to triumph, prevail, or subdue (Persian pîrûzî or fîrûzî), and qâhir, the corresponding name for one who does so (Persian pîrûz or fîrûz).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00505

The “archangelic Lights” that arise from the “sources of the Light of Glory and of the sovereignty of light” are called Anwâr qâhira: ruling or “victorial” Lights. (Recall the Greek Nikai mentioned above, and the Christian title Angelus victor, the victorious Angel, applied to the archangel Michael.) But an important distinction is needed here. The terms qahr and qâhir, together with their derivatives, also belong to the vocabulary of Arabic astrology, where they can even suggest the violence or domination exerted by a harmful star. Suhrawardi’s concept of Xvarnah certainly contains astrological allusions.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00506

Yet in the vocabulary of Eastern Theosophy, these terms carry no harmful or evil implication. We generally translate them with the adjective “victorial” rather than “victorious.” By “victorial” we mean an enduring quality of a being, a permanent capacity for triumph; “victorious” more readily suggests a victory already won. The word “victorial” was suggested to us by the Latin name Mons Victorialis, the “mountain of the dawns” from which, according to one Christian interpretation of Zoroastrian prophecies about the coming Saviour, the Magi set out on their journey. To designate this whole idea of “victorial power,” Suhrawardi may use the phrase al-amr al-qahrî: something like res victorialis, the reality or principle of victory.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00507

Perhaps we have now assembled the minimum background needed to understand the allusions, meanings, and implications of the texts in which the shaykh al-Ishrâq describes, in his turn, the different forms and appearances of the Light of Glory. These include the visions granted to the kings and prophet of ancient Persia, and the archangelic hierarchies that eternally “rise” from this Orient—from the highest Archangels down to the form of light nearest to each mystical pilgrim: his or her “Perfect Nature.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00508

At the end of the metaphysics of his great Book of Crossroads and Conversations, between the pages where he sets out the spiritual lineage of the Ishrâqîyûn and those where he alludes to events taking place in the mystical cities of the “intermediate Orient,” Suhrawardi gives a long account of the Xvarnah as both Light of Glory and personal Destiny. His threefold distinction corresponds to the three forms of manifestation described in the Avesta (see above, p. 86). He writes: 1) “If what is to predominate in the soul’s innermost being is the res victorialis (amr qahrî), then the effect of the dawning Light (shorûq) is to make the victorial powers (omûr qahrîya) prevail within it, powers arising from the configurations of the stars and from the Angels for whom those stars are the theurgies.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00509

“For the subtle reality that the ancient Persians (the Pahlawîyûn) called the Light of Glory (Khorrah, Xvarnah) has its source in the radiance of heaven, and its imprint upon the human soul is felt as victorial strength (qahr). The person invested with it thus becomes a hero, one who rules and triumphs. — 2) If the dawning Light springs from the sacred radiance of the pure spiritual Lights, in proportion to the soul’s capacity for ardent longing and love, then the imprint of the Light of Glory upon the soul makes its bearer find joy and happiness in things of delicacy and refinement.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00510

“Other souls feel spontaneously drawn towards such a person and come to love him, while peoples sing his praises, because the radiance investing him is transmitted from Angels whose theurgies are magnificent, worthy of reverence and love. — 3) Finally, if there is equilibrium, and the different forms of Light are abundantly present through the mediation of the lord who is the Sublime Luminary, then the person who possesses it is a revered king, one who inspires respect and is filled with knowledge, virtue, and happiness. This alone is called the ‘royal Light of Glory’ (Kayân-Khorrah). At its fullest, this last category is the most distinguished of the three, for it entails a perfect balance of Light; moreover, the Sublime Luminary is the gateway to all great ecstasies.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00511

Despite the particular nuances of Eastern Theosophy, we can recognise in this classification the three kinds of Light of Glory already distinguished in the Avesta. Suhrawardi’s first category corresponds to the Xvarnah of Iranian chivalry and legendary heroes.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00512
The second is the priestly spiritual gift of sacred souls, of men of God such as the prophet Zoroaster.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00513

The third is named directly in Persian: the royal Xvarnah, the “Glory of the Kayanids” (Kevaem Xvarenô). This is the Xvarnah in its fullness, bringing the other two together and tempering each with the other in a perfect balance of light.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00514
Three groups of observations may be offered:
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00515

In each case, the Light is transmitted through an intermediary, an idea belonging to astrology or to theosophy concerned with the stars. It is as though a flame were shining in heaven at the birth of the person to whom the Aura Gloriae is allotted and whom it invests. In the second and third categories, the “spiritual Lights” are specifically named as the intermediaries of the Xvarnah. In no case do the patterns of the stars or the heavenly bodies themselves act through some kind of mechanical causation. The active agents are what Suhrawardi’s angelology calls the Angels governing the theurgies (tilimsât)—that is, the bodies of every kind, whether in the earthly world or among the stars. These Angels mediate the “oriental source” (shorûq), the Light of Glory, from which they themselves arise and which belongs to the world beyond the senses. The royal Xvarnah, being the Xvarnah in its entirety, is mediated by the “Sublime Luminary” (al-Nayyir al-a‘zam), the sun. Once again, it is not the physical mass of the sun that acts in its own right, but the Angel who works through it, whom we shall later see Suhrawardi call by his Iranian name, Hûrakhsh. The sun is the gateway (pîshgâh) to the great ecstasies: Sol invictus, the unconquered Sun. We can thus discern a trace of Mithraism within the Ishrâq (see below, § 5, the psalm to the archangel of the Sun, and Chapter IV, 1).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00516

The three kinds of Xvarnah can readily be related to the three kinds of spiritual person, or philosopher-sage, mentioned in the prologue to the Book of Eastern Theosophy (see above, pp. 69 ff.). The first would be the Xvarnah of philosophers concerned solely with knowledge, heroes of the intellect. The second would belong to heroes of “theurgic piety,” or of pure mystical experience unmixed with philosophical knowledge. The third would belong to the person who combines both: the hero perfected alike in philosophical wisdom and in mystical and theurgic experience. Such a person is the Khalifat Allâh, God’s representative on His Earth (called precisely the Gubernator Terrae, “Governor of the Earth,” in the Corpus Hermeticum). The blessed king Kay Khosraw, as Suhrawardi contemplates him, was such a person. We might therefore see the passage from the first category to the third as the movement from heroic epic to mystical epic, a theme we shall develop later (Chapter IV, 4). The sages who follow in the footsteps of Kay Khosraw, the ecstatic king, are called the Khosrawânîyûn after him (the Persian adjective carries the general sense of royal or imperial). Kay Khosraw withdrew from this world into concealment after renouncing temporal rule. And Suhrawardi has expressly warned us that by “caliphal” authority he does not mean the exercise of worldly political power (see above, p. 71). The Xvarnah also invests the spiritual Pole when he is the “Hidden Imam,” invisible to the mass of humanity, although his light illuminates the hearts of the faithful and mysteriously guides them to the threshold of his dwelling in the “eighth clime” (see below, Book VII). Such are the Khosrawânîyûn. Suhrawardi’s vision gathers into one lineage of sacred figures the royal sage of ancient Persia and the mystical Imam (mystikos means “hidden”) of Shiite Persia. These features tell us much about the intentions of the shaykh al-Ishrâq.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00517

Elsewhere, too, Suhrawardi insists that the Lights encountered by the spiritual seeker, whose source is the Light of Glory, are not matters of theoretical knowledge or conceptual representation. Known in that way, the “oriental Source” would cease to be the Source; it would become simply one item of knowledge among others, an accidental property arising in the knowing subject. But this Source is the Orient of Knowledge itself, and its revelation touches the very depths of the being who encounters it. Suhrawardi makes this point at the end of one of his works written in Persian, the Partaw-Nâmeh, or Book of the Ray of Light, in a passage that concludes by clarifying once again the effects of the royal Xvarnah upon the soul.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00518

“These flashes and lights,” he says, “are not theoretical knowledge, nor are they representations formed by the intellect. No: they are sacred irradiations, emanating from the spiritual world. The spiritual world comprises all Lights existing apart from matter, and pure souls share in this splendour of light. There is no limit to the power and radiance of the light of the Necessary Being and of the Intelligence.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00519

“For souls in the other world, that light is more evident than anything visible to the eye in this world; it is more splendid than every splendour of light. The light of spiritual beings is not something added to their essence. No: they are Light, Light existing apart from matter, as the sages of Light have said on the strength of their own visionary experience.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00520

“Every sovereign who has been initiated into wisdom and perseveres in the worship and adoration of the Light of Lights is given the royal Light of Glory (Khorrah-e kayânî = Kayân-khorrah) and receives the royal splendour of Light (Farr-e nûrânî). The divine radiance clothes him in a robe of majesty and beauty. He is the natural leader of the world. He receives triumphant aid from the higher universe; his dreams and his inspiration attain perfection.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00521

We can now begin to understand the claim made by the shaykh al-Ishrâq when he bears witness to the vision granted to him, like the visions of Kay Khosraw, Zoroaster, and others—a vision upon which he would subsequently build his Eastern Theosophy.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
en-book-2-ch-3-s2
2. The Visions of Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00522

Suhrawardi alludes to the event that decisively changed the course of his spiritual life in a brief personal confession—one might even say a moment of self-criticism—at a crucial point in his Eastern Theosophy. He speaks of a direct vision that shattered both his doubts and the narrow limits within which he had confined himself in the company of the Peripatetic philosophers, the followers of Aristotle. It overturned the views he had favoured at the beginning of his career.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00523

As his commentators point out, he is referring to his adolescence, when he was taking his first steps in philosophy. The Peripatetic doctrine he then defended was a cosmology that limited the number of angelic Intelligences moving the celestial Spheres to ten, or at most fifty-five.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00524
Now he clearly understands his youthful error.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00525

However wonderful the order and relationships governing the world of bodies—the world of night and darkness—those governing the world of the noble and pure Lights must be prior to them and higher than them. What can the Peripatetic philosophers possibly do with a plenitude of Intelligences restricted to such a paltry number? No: the relationships and proportions reigning in the world of Light are infinitely more wonderful, more real, and more complex than those we discover in our world, which is only their projected shadow.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00526

The first thing Suhrawardi rejected, then, was a cosmology that knew nothing of worlds inhabited by countless beings of light. The conversion of the shaykh al-Ishrâq was bound up with a revelation of the world of angels. As he would repeatedly recall, it was above all this angelic world that inspired the thought and shaped the worship of the ancient Persians.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00527

We should note something else: Suhrawardi had an intuition of the unfathomable wonders of the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars,” a term that also encompasses all the star systems and galaxies beyond our solar system. His discovery of angelology went hand in hand with an astronomical revolution that burst open the limited heavens of Aristotelian and Ptolemaic astronomy. In the West, by contrast, the astronomical revolution came at the expense of angelology. This is no small indication of the difference between our cultures.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00528

Suhrawardi knows that the pure spiritual Lights have been contemplated by all those who, at one time or another, have shed the dwelling of their physical bodies like an outer skin, and have then put their testimony into writing to guide others. This is what all the accounts of ecstasy describe: those of Hermes, Empedocles, and Plato. Plato, too, recounted his own experience and testified that, having cast off the darkness, he had directly beheld the world of Light.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00529

We already know, of course, that under Plato’s name Suhrawardi is referring to the celebrated ecstasy of Plotinus. He knew it through the account from the Enneads embedded in the work called the Theology of Aristotle, a paraphrase of Plotinus. Throughout his Eastern Theosophy he returns repeatedly to this famous account: “Plato” (that is, Plotinus) said, “When I was separated from my material body, I saw Spheres of light.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00530

The commentators explain that these words refer to the highest archangelic Intelligences. Those of more intense light encompass those whose light is weaker, just as the heavenly Spheres in traditional astronomy are nested one within another. Suhrawardi then sums up the Plotinian account: “Plato related of himself that, in certain spiritual states, he seemed to be stripped of his body and separated from the material condition. Then he contemplated Light and Beauty within himself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00531

“Next he rose towards the divine Cause that embraces all things. He felt as though he had been placed within it, suspended from it, and he contemplated the Sublime Light on the highest divine summit.” This is the substance of the account, down to its conclusion: “But then conscious reflection came to place a veil between me and that Light.” For his part, the prophet who gave the law to the Arabs and Persians (the prophet Muhammad) declared: “God has seventy-seven veils of light; if they were lifted from before His Face, the radiance of His Face would set ablaze everything His gaze encompasses.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00532

A few pages earlier, Suhrawardi had already invoked the ecstatic testimonies of Hermes and Plato, and concluded: “The sages of Persia and India, too, are unanimous on this point. Well, if in astronomy we take account of observations made by one or two people, how can we fail to take account of the explicit testimony of those who were pillars of wisdom and prophecy, concerning something they themselves had seen directly in the course of their spiritual observations?”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00533

For Suhrawardi, this is the decisive argument, and a modern phenomenologist could hardly put it better. We recognise that the first condition for a phenomenon—that which shows itself—is the capacity of the person to whom it shows itself. The objectivity of the vision is inseparable from this relationship.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00534

Those to whom the phenomenon remains hidden have only one possible course: to discover the conditions under which it becomes visible to those who see it. That is why something like our word “phenomenology” may long have existed in the Arabic expression kashf al-mahjûb, the act of unveiling or disclosing what is hidden. The phrase appears in the titles of many works of mystical knowledge and experience. Any other criticism of the visionary object fails to reach that object and prejudges the manner of its existence.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00535

All attempts to explain away the reality of what was seen by giving it a causal “explanation,” reducing it to a meaning that falls short of the reality that shows itself—none of this interests Suhrawardi. He will always counter with the prior question: by what right can those who have not seen reject the testimony of those who have? In his Glosses on these pages, Mulla Sadra Shirazi recalls the existence of an otherworldly faculty of sight (hiss basarî okhrawî), the organ that perceives the Malakût, the angelic world.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00536

Those who lack it can always deny what others see, but their denial carries no weight. Drawing strength from the testimonies he invokes, especially those of the sages of ancient Persia, whose theosophical wisdom he sought to revive, the shaykh al-Ishrâq explains himself in these words:
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00537

“The author of these lines” (that is, Suhrawardi himself) “began as a staunch defender of the Peripatetic doctrine that denied these things, because he was excessively attached to their teaching. And he would have persisted in that position if he had not himself seen the decisive proof given by his Lord.” As the commentators emphasise, this was indeed a direct vision, a visionary perception of the pure Lights.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00538

The author saw that all the forms, figures, and species existing in our world are icons or images (asnâm), shadows and silhouettes (ashbâh), of immaterial forms of light existing in the world of Intelligence. Suhrawardi continues: “If someone refuses to believe this testimony and finds this proof insufficient, let him undertake spiritual exercises in his turn and become a pupil of masters gifted with visionary perception.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00539

“Perhaps an ecstatic vision will come to him, showing him the Light that pours forth in the world of the Jabarût (the world of the cherubic Intelligences). Perhaps he will see the celestial beings of the Malakût (the world of the Angels who are the ‘lords of species,’ or archetypes; see below). Perhaps he will contemplate the Lights contemplated by Hermes and Plato: the spiritual splendours, sources of the Light of Glory and of the Sovereignty of Light, which Zoroaster proclaimed and towards which the most truthful king, the blessed Kay Khosraw, was carried in an ecstasy that allowed him to behold them directly.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00540

“The sages of ancient Persia were so unanimous about this that, according to them, Water has an archetypal Angel (sâhib al-sanam) in the world of the Malakût, whom they called Khordâd (Avestan Haurvatât). Plants have an Angel, whom they called Môrdâd (Avestan Ameretât). Fire has an Angel, whom they called Ordibehest (Avestan Arta Vahishta). These are also the Lights to which Empedocles and several other sages alluded.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00541

We have emphasised the characteristic expression “sources of the Light of Glory and of the Sovereignty of Light.” Suhrawardi combines two Persian technical terms in an Arabic phrase, yanâbî’ al-Khorrah wa’l-Rây. The first is already familiar to us (Avestan xvarnah, Pahlavi xvarrah).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00542

The second, rây, represents an Avestan term (rayi) suggesting royal greatness, splendour, and magnificence. The pairing of the two terms, or of the adjectives derived from them, is both traditional and characteristic in the Avesta and the Pahlavi texts. Their appearance here is therefore evidence that Suhrawardi is not inventing anything. He is following a tradition that, by one route or another, had reached the man who would “revive the wisdom of ancient Persia.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00543

Elsewhere in the book, other expressions likewise allude to these “sources of the Light of Glory.” As we have said, Eastern Theosophy begins with a radical reform of Logic and ends with something like a reminder of ecstasy, interrupted by two lyrical psalms. There we hear of “wanderers who come knocking at the gateway of the lofty halls of Light.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00544

The “Angels who draw them towards the Orient” come out to meet them and pour upon them Water flowing from the “Source of Beauty” (Yanbû’ al-bahâ’). We have already noted (p. 92 above) that Xvarnah can also be translated into Arabic as bahâ’, meaning beauty, radiance, or splendour. Here, then, the “Source of Beauty” is equivalent to the Yanâbî’ al-Khorrah, the Sources of the Light of Glory, in the great passage of Suhrawardi’s personal confession.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00545

The description of the Angels in that same passage makes it especially clear that, in his thought, Xvarnah and Ishrâq, Light of Glory and Light of the Orient, Source of the Xvarnah and oriental Source, can express the same reality. Water and Light, too, are traditionally interchangeable symbols of the sources of Life and Knowledge. Elsewhere we encounter the expressions “Sources of Life” and “Sources of Light and Life.” The Source is not itself an object of knowledge; it is what makes knowledge spring forth.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00546

Naturally, these passages particularly engaged Suhrawardi’s earliest commentators, Shahrazuri and Qotb Shirazi. Their explanations show us what they knew of ancient Persian spirituality. Both specify that the “spiritual splendours” Suhrawardi speaks of—these heavenly irradiations—are those proclaimed by the prophet, “the wise, excellent and perfect Imam Zoroaster of Azerbaijan.” In his “Zend Book,” Zoroaster declares that the world is divided into two realms: mînôvî, the world of Light, the spiritual world, and gêtî, the dark, bodily world. These are indeed the two great cosmological categories of the Avesta: mainyava and gaethya (Pahlavi mênôk and gêtîk).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00547

From the world of Light, a Light streams over the souls of the Perfect. It supports them, granting splendour and strength (ta’yîd and rây); their souls are filled with its radiance, and over them rises a dawn more brilliant than the rising sun. “It is this Light that is called Khorrah in Pahlavi, as Zoroaster also says: the Khorrah is a Light streaming from the divine Essence. Through it, creatures are ordered in a hierarchy in which some take precedence over others, while its aid establishes each creature in its proper action and work. The Khorrah belonging to sovereigns is called Kayân Khorrah.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00548

Thus a fundamental idea of Mazdean theosophy re-entered the stream of Islamic mystical knowledge and theosophy. From generation to generation, the Ishrâqîyûn, heirs to the Khosrawânîyûn, would pass on what Suhrawardi and his commentators had bequeathed to them.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00549

Alongside the prophet Zoroaster, the “blessed king Kay Khosraw” is named here once again. Kay Khosraw is indeed the dominant and final figure of the Kayanid dynasty before the appearance of Vishtaspa, Zoroaster’s protector. Each of the Kayanids has particular traits and a distinctive story, rich in heroic and turbulent detail.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00550

Yet none can be fitted into our chronologies. They belong forever to their own time—a time which, through Kay Khosraw, also belongs to all the Khosrawânîyûn sages. A few pages from now this commanding figure will reappear, his “history” passing beyond history into the “eighth clime.” That clime beyond all climes is the place where the heroic epic secretly passes into the mystical epic. It is also the place where a meeting becomes possible between the mystical chivalry of Iran as Suhrawardi understands it—the initiated Khosrawânîyûn, that is, the Ishrâqîyûn—and the chivalry of our own Grail tradition (see below, Chapters IV and V).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00551

A passage Suhrawardi devotes elsewhere to Kay Khosraw shows us the sacred character he sees in the Iranian sovereign, placed in the line of ecstatic heroes stretching from Hermes to Empedocles. All the commentators, naturally, reproduced this passage. “It happened,” writes our shaykh, “that Kay Khosraw the Blessed remained absorbed in prayer and long inward meditation.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00552

“Then the Wisdom (Sophia) of the most holy Father came to him and spoke with him of the world of Mystery (ghayb, the unmanifest). He was carried away into the highest world; his soul received the imprint of divine Sophia; the archangelic Lights appeared to him face to face, and in that encounter he understood the nature of the subtle reality called the royal Light of Glory (Kayân-Khorrah): it is the casting (ilqâ’) into the soul of a victorial element (qâhir) before which heads bow down.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00553

Kay Khosraw’s visionary ecstasy is therefore of the same kind as the ecstasies that brought Zoroaster face to face with the divine Heptad during his conversations with the “Archangels,” the Seven Most Holy Immortals. Kay Khosraw’s conversations with heavenly Wisdom also recall the conversations of the sage recorded in the Pahlavi book entitled Mênôke-Xrat (Heavenly Wisdom).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00554

Yet the long passages Ferdowsi devotes to Kay Khosraw’s exploits in the Shâh-Nâmeh fall far short of what Suhrawardi writes about the ecstatic hero’s calling. The same is true of the other heroes of the Iranian epic who appear in his Mystical Narratives (see below, Chapters IV and V). That, precisely, is the mission of the shaykh al-Ishrâq as the bearer of ancient Persia’s spiritual inheritance: to lead its heroes to the fulfilment of their vocation, to become their history himself, and to decipher the mystery concealed from us by Kay Khosraw’s final disappearance.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00555

Without crossing the threshold of death, Kay Khosraw vanishes from the sight of the people of this world, just as the twelfth and last Imam of Shiism will later become invisible to them, thereafter to be known as the Awaited One.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00556

Kay Khosraw is the figure of the initiate who has become a perfect Sage, initiated by Wisdom—heavenly Sophia herself. This investiture consecrates him as the mystical King of the world, endowed above all with what the Neoplatonist Iamblichus called the “sacred virtues.” It is when Kay Khosraw becomes invisible to human eyes that he is truly the mystical sovereign. “Casting a victorial element into the soul”: the Form of Light that is the Perfect Nature also casts forms of knowledge into Hermes. And the Hermetic initiate likewise became Gubernator Terrae, Governor of the Earth.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00557

How is the initiate—who, according to Suhrawardi’s deepest wish, seeks both philosophical knowledge and mystical experience—to reach the fulfilment of his desires? Suhrawardi teaches him what oriental knowledge is and points out where its oriental Source lies.
